build.reason:
This falls under BUILD_BRIEF step 7 ("no target whose computation can be split into a chain"), as BATCH5_PREREGISTRATION anticipates for short wrappers. The only allowed target, FromStringDeserializer.types(), cannot carry C10 validly, for four reasons.

(1) Nothing to redistribute. types() has no parameters and no computation. Its body is `return new Class<?>[] { File.class, ..., InetSocketAddress.class };`, a constant list in Std.STD_* kind order. It has no argument guard, no iteration, no decision and no per-element core, so the chain has nothing to place in hops 1-4 and nothing to put in a gold. Any five-hop chain would invent a computation whose output is a constant.

(2) No valid fault. With no input, any omission changes the returned set by a fixed amount. The only single-test effect is dropping one class, for example Charset -> TestJdkTypes::testCharset. That needs the gold to give one specific class a treatment the other eleven do not get. Two shapes are possible, and neither works:
- A per-class or per-kind enumeration (a switch over STD_FILE..STD_INET_SOCKET_ADDRESS, or an if-chain like findDeserializer): dropping one case is a T3(a) trace, a closed set fixed by the type code, with siblings handled.
- A uniform copy or filter loop: an omission hits all 12 elements or none. A frozen write position (T2(b)(ii)) or null entries (an NPE in JdkDeserializers.<clinit>, then ExceptionInInitializerError and NoClassDefFoundError across the suite) breaks gate G5; dropping a supported-class filter changes nothing.
A no-arg gold that holds the literal and loses one line of it is not an omission "in an iteration or decision".

(3) No single owner. Every hop above the gold holds the complete constant data and can add a dropped class back in one line. So can the only production caller, JdkDeserializers' static initializer, which already keeps its own parallel literal list (UUID, AtomicBoolean, StackTraceElement, ByteBuffer). The effect can therefore be recovered by a caller, which C10 forbids.

(4) No test calls the facade. The pool's "test_files: 6" comes from a name-based substring match on test method names (testNestedUntypes in TestUntypedDeserialization, testSubtypes in TestCreatorWithPolymorphic113, testPropertyWithSubtypes in TestSubtypes). The only call site of types() is JdkDeserializers.<clinit> (JdkDeserializers.java:25), which runs once per JVM and is reached only through BasicDeserializerFactory.findDefaultDeserializer.

build.gold: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.deser.BasicDeserializerFactory::simpleTypeOf(Class<?> cls), file src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/BasicDeserializerFactory.java. Correct version: a class with no super-class (Object, an interface or a primitive) gets the bare SimpleType.constructUnsafe(cls). Any other class gets a walk up its super-class chain to the root (Object), and the root's bare type is then narrowed to cls with forcedNarrowBy, so SimpleType._narrow links every super-class level. This gives the original result field for field.

build.fault: The while loop that moves base from the immediate super-class up to the chain root is omitted (3 lines). The type is then narrowed from the bare type of the immediate super-class. That super-class's type has no super class of its own, and AnnotatedClass._findFields skips the fields of such a type. So Point's field x is lost for Point3D, while direct children of Object are unaffected.

build.reason:
The recipe needs a one-line omission in the gold, inside an iteration or decision that no caller can pre-filter or recover. Exactly one existing test must catch it, and the whole variant gold must pass T1-T4. Period.fieldDifference (Period.java:256-276) offers no such fault.

(1) Validation faults are ruled out. The original's only decisions are: the null test, the size test, start.getFieldType(i) != end.getFieldType(i), and the adjacent duplicate-duration test. All four are argument validation, and the fixed facade javadoc states each one ('must not be null', 'The two partials must contain the same fields', 'may not contain overlapping fields', '@throws IllegalArgumentException if the partials are null or invalid'). So the same check at the facade, or at any pass-through hop, matches all documentation. It also copies the guard shape of the evidence methods (BasePeriod's partial constructor, BaseSingleFieldPeriod.between, AbstractPartial.compareTo). That makes it a competing repair.
- The gold cannot claim the check with an @throws clause, because the variant would then state a throw it never makes (T4).
- The overlap check is also redundant: PeriodType.forFields already rejects repeated duration types.
- This holds for tests 2, 3, 4 and 5.

(2) Computational faults are ruled out. The only test that checks a computed result is testFactoryFieldDifference1 (it checks -1Y 2M -2D and the type PeriodType.yearMonthDay()). Its result depends only on the per-field subtraction and the period type. Every one-line omission there either leaves a local trace or can be recovered by a caller:
- Dropping either operand of end.getValue(i) - start.getValue(i): T3(b), one half of the start/end pair is treated and the other is not; with a precomputed base array, T1.
- Dropping the duration-type derivation or a loop step: T2 (a dead or frozen local).
- Dropping PeriodType.forFields(types), so new MutablePeriod() is used: this is not in an iteration or decision. A caller can recover it with withPeriodType at the placement hop. Test 5 also newly fails, unless the overlap check moves into the guard. With setValue(i) writing by position, types becomes dead or the result is visibly mis-placed (T2 or T4).
- Index-to-type mapping (setValue(i) vs set(type) vs indexOf): makes no difference, because Partial's largest-first order always matches the standard period order. No test can see it.

(3) No equivalent restatement adds a needed step that is not a trace (reset, special value, boundary or delimiter):
- add(end) then add(-start): the omission is one half of a pair (T3).
- Reading end by type with end.get(fieldType): this is the same validation again.
- Partial-to-period then Period.minus: no step left to omit.
- Clearing a period passed in to be filled: only matters if a hop pre-fills it, which is contrived.
- Weekyear or halfday mapping, chronology conversion: change the original semantics, and test 1 cannot reach them.

So, under BUILD_BRIEF steps 7 and 'Pre-run checks', this target cannot carry the recipe without a competing owner or a local trace.

The default-provider resolution (property, then bundled data, then UTC) moves into the chain with its core in the gold. Validation and installation stay in setProvider0, because they write DateTimeZone's private static state.

Omitting the property attempt gives a variant gold with no local trace. testProvider is the only test that reaches the chain past the permission check and the only one that sets the property. Its finally blocks restore the default provider, so no other test sees the change.

The convention is pinned outside the gold:

2. The omission is a whole 9-line try/catch: one decision step, but larger than a single line.

3. Three edits outside the gold pass the trigger and the full suite (checked in scratch copies, 0 failing tests each). I recorded all three as bypasses:

A reviewer who reads hop 4 ('using the default zone provider when none is specified') as responsible for the property could call B-2 a competing repair.

(b) Hops 1-3 are pass-throughs. Hop 4 does what its doc says. The declared hop edits still fail the trigger.

T1.why: The method `defaultZoneProvider()` takes no parameters, so no input can fail to matter.

T2.why: The only locals are `ex`, passed as a call argument to `uncaughtException`, and `thread`, used as the call receiver and argument, so neither is dead or frozen; the try/catch has no if/else, switch or ternary, and its catch block has a real side effect, so there is no dead decision.

T4.why: The javadoc ("Gets the default zone provider" / "@return the default zone provider") only describes in general terms what the method computes, the body does return a provider on every path, and the javadoc names no concrete rule, limit, value class or case that the code visibly breaks.

build.reason:
GJChronology.getInstance cannot carry the C10 recipe validly at the Time-18 fixed revision (b609d7d6). The real Time-18 bug is in getDateTimeMillis, not the factory, and this revision does not yet have the cutover-too-early check in getInstance that later revisions add. The factory's computation has five steps: zone normalisation, cutover default, per-zone list lookup or creation, the reverse search for an entry with matching min days and cutover, and build-on-miss (UTC base or zoned wrapper) followed by caching.

I applied each possible one-step omission to the original method and ran the full suite. Every omission with an observable effect fails at least 2 tests, so gate G5 cannot pass. The cache is identity-based, because GJChronology.equals falls through to Object.equals. Any omission in the cache-insert, search or build steps therefore breaks assertSame/assertEquals in 22-23 tests across TestSerialization, TestCalendarConverter, TestInterval and others. The null-cutover default is reached through BuddhistChronology and CalendarConverter, and omitting it fails 52 tests.

The closest case is the null-zone default, with 2 failing tests. It also fails single-owner: any hop documented "null is default" can repair it in one line with DateTimeUtils.getZone(zone). It is an argument normalisation, not a per-element core.

Dropping either term of the cache-match test fails 3 tests, and it would also be a checklist T3 trace (a match key built from one of the two parameters the gold reads).

The four delegating overloads have no decision of their own. The long overload's only decision (default millis → null) has no observable effect when omitted (0 failing tests), because the new Instant equals DEFAULT_CUTOVER.

Since the correct configuration must reproduce the original result for every input, no other step is available to omit. Per brief step 7 ("no fault that only one test catches"), the instance is UNBUILDABLE.

build.concerns:
1. Ownership depends on reading the contract the hh:mm way. The gold says "offset to UTC in hours and minutes" with minutes "from 0 to 59", and (-2, 30) means -02:30 (-150 min). A purely additive reading (-2 h + 30 min = -01:30) would make the variant look right. The hh:mm convention is pinned outside the gold by:
- the facade javadoc: "The minutes value is always positive... (-2, 30) ... '-02:30'";
- DateTimeFormatterBuilder$TimeZoneOffset.parseInto, which applies the sign to hours+minutes, pinned by testForID_String ("-07:05:34.0");
- ZoneInfoCompiler.parseTime, pinned by TestCompiler::testCompile;
- DateTimeZone.printOffset.
An auditor who weighs the additive reading could still return FLAG_AMBIGUOUS.

2. Recorded one-line hop edits that pass the trigger and the full suite on the variant (each checked in a scratch copy, 0 failures):
- B-0: a hop computes the offset itself and calls forOffsetMillis (bypass).
- B-1, mirror at hop 4: `hours < 0 ? DateTimeZone.forOffsetMillis(-LocalDate.zoneFromOffsetFields(-hours, minutes).getOffset(0L)) : ...`. I classified it as a bypass, but this is the most likely place for an auditor to disagree. The hop takes over the sign decision, never asks the gold about (-2, 30), and discards the gold's zone for a new one; the precedent is Math-55 B-1, "a second implementation of the gold's decision".
- B-2: hop 4 passes signed minutes. It breaks the documented minutes range of 0 to 59 and gives -01:30 on the correct gold.
- B-3: hop 4 borrows an hour (hours - 1, 60 - minutes). It asks for '-03:30' and gives -03:30 on the correct gold.
B-2 and B-3 are inconsistent with the documentation only under the hh:mm reading.

3. The gold returns a DateTimeZone, not a number. This was deliberate: with a numeric result, a hop could fix the output by simply negating it. As a result the gold holds all of the original arithmetic, hops 3 and 4 are pure pass-throughs, and forOffsetMillis now sits inside hop 1's try block. That is behaviour-preserving, because forOffsetMillis never throws ArithmeticException.

4. The lie names forTimeZone, which is a real method but not a hop. It might steer a reader toward parseOffset or forTimeZone, which hold evidence-like code.

5. The evidence entry for the nested class is written in binary-name form, org.joda.time.format.DateTimeFormatterBuilder$TimeZoneOffset::parseInto. The metric catalog may spell nested classes differently; this affects only the secondary evidence_displayed measure.

Applied to the whole variant gold, and earlier to the correct gold, where nothing needed rewriting.

T2 absent: hoursInMinutes is read by the next line and offsetMinutes by the return. Both are computed from the parameters, not set from literals. There is no loop, branch, case or ternary.
T3 absent: no sign, case, range-end or value-class test remains, so no member of any set is handled. The two fields of the offset, hours and minutes, are both read and both go into the sum.

build.reason:
getDefault cannot carry the C10 recipe validly; brief step 7 and the BUILD_BRIEF line "if no valid fault without a local trace exists for your target, report UNBUILDABLE".

(1) Only one input reaches the computation. Apart from the cache, getDefault's only behaviour is the lazy resolution: the user.timezone property via forID, then the JDK default via forTimeZone, then UTC. Under Defects4J that resolution sees one fixed input in every run (single test or full suite, every class): the property and the JDK default are both America/Los_Angeles. Every other path returns what setDefault stored, and production code reads it everywhere (ISOChronology.getInstance, DateTimeUtils.getZone, forID(null), forTimeZone(null)). So a change on the cached path breaks thousands of tests, which fails gate G5.

(2) The only sensitive test reacts to "fixed zone or not". Exactly one existing test, testSetInto_Object, reacts to the lazy result, and only to whether the zone is fixed (probes P1-P4). A valid fault must therefore turn the most ordinary input, a region id the provider knows given twice, into a fixed zone. The three ways to do that all fail:
- Keep the original structure. The only omission that yields UTC is dropping the `temp == null` test before the UTC fallback. The values resolved from the property and the JDK zone are then overwritten on every path: checklist T1 and T2(a).
- Route both sources through one gold resolver and drop the region lookup. That step is the main case of forID and forTimeZone (callee logic, not the facade's computation). The gold would visibly resolve only UTC and offset ids, which is not a quiet gold and risks T3/T4.
- Restructure into a loop over the sources and drop its early exit, so the last recognised source (UTC) wins. Hops 1-4 hold the sources and can filter them or apply the fallback themselves, so callers can absorb the fault and repair it at hop 4. The gold can only be made the single owner if its javadoc states which source takes precedence, and that phrase is T4 on the variant.

(3) The facade cannot become "guard plus one delegating call" without a recipe deviation or a change in meaning. The cache field cDefault is private and no drawn host can write it. The facade would have to keep the double-checked lazy init itself, or the chain would have to stop caching. Not caching contradicts the facade's own NOTE that a later change to the java.util.TimeZone default is not picked up.

build.reason:
The two-argument overload resolves './' and '../' names, and only testModuleName exercises that; every other require in the suite is a top-level name. The URI resolution was redistributed as follows: extension removal, then the relative/top-level decision, then the directory of the requiring file, then the split into parts without '.', then the gold's walk.

The '..' step needs the path walked so far, and only the gold's loop has it. A step done on whole strings (dashes, extension, leading './') could be applied before or after the chain by any hop, so it would not be a valid single-owner fault.

The correct chain gives the same result as the original for every top-level name and for every CommonJS-form relative name (made of '.', '..' and plain names). That includes a '..' that climbs above the first directory, which is kept as java.net.URI keeps it. It differs only on names no caller or test passes: repeated separators, queries, colons, or a name ending in '.' or '..'.
build.concerns:
1. No passing test other than the trigger pins the '..' convention. It is pinned by code outside the gold: the facade's javadoc ("relative addressing with ./ and ../"), hop 2's dispatch of '../' names, and PathUtil.collapseDots/makeAbsolute/makeRelative. The ownership tests (testWithoutExports, testDash, testGuessModuleName, CompilerTest.testCommonJSProvidesAndRequire) pin neighbouring conventions on the same path. An auditor applying (f) strictly could object.

2. Hop 4 leaves out the '.' parts, which is a dot-part rule just above the gold. A careful reader could see hop 4 as the place for '..' too. A one-line '..' fix there needs PathUtil.collapseDots plus an empty directory (B-2).

3. Three one-line bypasses were checked on the variant in scratch copies; each passed the trigger with 0 failing tests in the full suite:
- B-1: hop 2 returns toModuleName(PathUtil.makeAbsolute(name, dir)), which makes hops 3-5 dead.
- B-2: hop 4 passes the gold "" and the parts of collapseDots(dir + "/" + name), replacing the gold's walk.
- B-3: a test-fitted regex rewrite of the module name.

Both PathUtil versions drop a '..' that climbs above the first directory, which URI keeps. I classify all three as bypass or test-fitted, but an auditor could argue that B-2 is a competing repair.

4. The gold builds the module name itself rather than calling toModuleName(String). This avoids having the intact overload, whose javadoc says "JS identifier", turn "foo/../baz" into a non-identifier on the trigger path. The cost is that the gold repeats the naming steps.

5. The correct chain is a manual walk, not java.net.URI. It is exact only on the documented domain.

6. This is a facade reuse of Closure-9, so the instance is not independent of that group.

7. The caching lie is plausible but contradicted by the code: no table exists anywhere.

8. The removed java.net imports leave one blank line among the imports of ProcessCommonJSModules.

(a) Only the gold breaks its own contract: moduleNameOfParts("foo", [..,baz]) returns module$foo$..$baz. Each hop does what its javadoc says.
(b) No hop javadoc contradicts its code. Hop 4 leaves out only '.' parts, so '..' goes to the gold.
(c) Declared edits fail the trigger. collapseDots at hop 3 or 4, URI.resolve at hop 2 and a leading-'..' loop at hop 4 pass the full suite. All are bypasses: they re-implement the gold's walk or leave hops unused.
(d) Neutral names; the caching lie does not mention dots.

(f) Pinned by the facade javadoc, hop 2's javadoc and PathUtil.collapseDots. No passing test pins '..'.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the main computation: `dir` seeds `new StringBuilder(dir)`, and every element of `parts` is appended through `path.append(part)`, so both reach the returned string.

T2.why: The locals `path` and `part` both reach the return value. The only decision, `if (path.length() > 0)`, changes the output: it leaves out the separator before the first part when `dir` is empty. So nothing is dead, frozen or a dead decision.

T3.why: The gold's text closes no set that it handles only in part. The two replacements (separator to "$", "-" to "_") belong to no set the gold names, and it names no format, enum or two-member pair that is partly treated. Path-part classes such as "." or ".." are not named and none is handled, so the "no member handled" exclusion applies.

T4.why: "without a trailing separator" is a caller precondition on `dir`. "the module name of the file that the parts lead to" is a general description that the body's join-and-replace lines do address. No phrase names a concrete rule that the code visibly breaks.

build.concerns:
1. A test-fitted one-statement loop at hop 4 passes the trigger and the full suite (checked on the variant in a scratch copy). It loops over the root's children and calls the gold only on those that are not functions. It still enters a function nested one block deeper, so hop 4's documented result does not hold. It is recorded as B-1 in the design and in ownership_reason. An auditor could weigh it toward FLAG_AMBIGUOUS. No suite test can rule it out: any test that would expose it would also catch the fault and break G5.
2. A one-physical-line post-filter loop at hop 4 also passes the suite (B-2). It is an iterator over the map that removes nodes NodeUtil.has cannot reach without entering a function. It is a second implementation of the exclusion, and it drops the branch's own var when a nested function declares the same name first ('function g(){var a;} var a;').
3. The NAME-as-leaf rule is a change of form from the original, which also descended into var initializers. Without it the fault would also fail FoldConstantsTest::testVarLifting.
4. The contract violation depends on JS scoping: 'the vars declared in a branch' does not include a nested function's vars. A blind checker could read that phrase as T4. I judged it a general description, like the checklist's own 'a valid variable name' example.
5. The facade is reused from Closure-137.
6. VarCollector is removed by a pre-edit. G1 shows this is behaviour-preserving.
7. The lie (level-by-level flattening plus an alphabetical sort) cannot be refuted by any test, because the trigger compares sets. Only reading the code shows it is false.

audit.summary:
CONFIRMED.
(a) Only the gold, Compiler$CodeBuilder::addBranchVars, walks the tree and decides whether to descend. On the trigger it records foo, a var of the nested anonymous function. Hops 1-4 only pass results through, so their outputs are wrong by inheritance.
(b) Every hop's javadoc matches its body.
(c) No competing repair. The one-line hop-4 child loop passes the full suite but still collects vars of deeper-nested functions. A hop-1 post-filter loses shadowed branch vars. The hop-2 filtering map and the hop-4 re-walk are bypasses. The declared compensating edits still fail the trigger.
(d) Names are neutral, and the lie names neither functions nor scopes.
(e) The gold is five calls down, in five distinct existing classes. The facade is one delegating call with one false sentence. Only the trigger fails.
(f) Pinned by SyntacticScopeCreator.scanVars, the redeclareVarsInsideBranch javadoc, testFunctionScope and testVarLifting.

T1.why: Both parameters feed the main computation: `n` decides the NAME test, supplies the parent, the key and the stored value, and drives the recursion, and `vars` is read by `containsKey` and written by `put`.

T2.why: The local `parent` is read in the condition that decides whether the live `vars.put` runs, the loop cursor `c` advances with `c = c.getNext()`, no local is set to a literal and left unchanged, and neither branch is empty, a no-op or the same as the other.

T3.why: The gold handles exactly one declaration kind (`Token.VAR`). It names no larger closed set of declaration kinds and no other member of one, so by the closure rule this is one member of a larger unnamed set (not T3), and there is no pair or partly handled named class.

T4.why: The concrete javadoc phrases are all met in the body: "the NAME node" by `n.getType() == Token.NAME` and `vars.put(n.getString(), n)`, and "first declaration" by `!vars.containsKey(n.getString())`. "vars declared in a branch" is a general description that the VAR-parent test and the recursion do address.
